claims.text: The modified material is an equimolar W-Ta-Ti-V-Zr high-entropy alloy.
Atomic-size and modulus mismatch among W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr produces local lattice distortions.
The local lattice distortions produce heterogeneous nanoscale internal stress fields.
The distortion-induced stress fields alter dislocation nucleation.
The distortion-induced stress fields alter dislocation pinning.
The distortion-induced stress fields alter dynamic recovery.
Enhanced dislocation storage and dynamic recovery enable more uniform plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation delays catastrophic failure.
The proposed dislocation mechanism increases plastic strain in WTaTiVZr relative to commercially used pure tungsten at high temperature.
The proposed dislocation mechanism increases toughness in WTaTiVZr relative to commercially used pure tungsten at high temperature.
The HEA and pure-tungsten specimens will be prepared with identical grain-size distributions to reduce microstructural confounding.
Testing in vacuum or inert gas at approximately 1200 degrees Celsius simulates relevant plasma-facing-component service conditions.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr is predicted to exhibit a higher dislocation density during high-temperature tensile deformation.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr is predicted to exhibit more uniform and extensive plastic deformation.
Relative to pure tungsten, WTaTiVZr is predicted to exhibit higher tensile strain-to-failure.
Ex situ analyses are predicted to show features consistent with enhanced dynamic recovery in WTaTiVZr.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply between approximately 1100 and 1300 degrees Celsius when grain size and other microstructural variables are controlled.
Precipitation or departure from a single-phase solid-solution state may alter the mechanical behavior.
Significant processing differences may alter the observed mechanical behavior.
Electronic-structure modifications may contribute to the mechanical response in addition to lattice distortion.
